script.title: Holiday spending without the January regret: a complete plan
script.hook: Every January, millions of people open a credit card statement and wonder how December happened. This year, let's make sure that isn't you.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: Every January, a lot of people open a credit card statement and wonder how December happened. It's rarely one big purchase. It's forty small ones, spread across gifts, travel, food and a few things nobody planned for. So in this video, we're building a holiday spending plan from scratch. It takes about thirty minutes, and by the end you'll have one total, four category numbers, a per-person gift number, and a plan so next December is already paid for. No guilt, no spreadsheets you'll abandon. Just a plan you can actually follow.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes sitting by a window with snow outside, a notebook and a mug of cocoa. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The one total
segments.narration: Start with one number: how much can you spend this holiday season from money you already have or will earn this month? Not next month's paycheck, and not a credit card balance you'll pay off 'eventually'. Look at your checking account, subtract your bills through the end of the month and a small cushion, and see what's left. Add anything you've already set aside. That's your ceiling. If that number feels small, that's useful information, not a failure. A smaller holiday you can pay for beats a bigger one that follows you into March.
segments.on_screen_text: Step 1: one total you can pay now
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a single large envelope with a coin inside and a December calendar behind it. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Four categories
segments.narration: Now split that total into four categories. One: gifts. Two: travel, door to door, including gas, parking, rideshares to the airport and the pet sitter. Three: food and hosting, like groceries for a big meal, the dish you bring to a potluck, drinks. Four: extras. This is the category people forget: outfits for parties, decorations, tips for building staff or the mail carrier, the white elephant gift, the ugly sweater. Give each one a number. If they add up to more than your total, shrink the biggest one first, because that's where the room usually is.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. four envelopes in a row with small icons: a gift, a suitcase, a pie and a string of lights. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Per-person gifts
segments.narration: Next, gifts. Write down every single name. Family, friends, partner, coworkers, secret Santa, the host of the party you're going to. Then divide your gift total by the number of names. Say you have three hundred dollars and twelve people. That's twenty-five each. That per-person number makes every decision easy. When you see something for forty, you already know the answer: pick something else, or deliberately take fifteen from someone else's budget. Some people get more, some get less. That's fine, as long as you decide it on purpose instead of at the register.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a long list of names with small gift boxes of equal size beside each. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Cheaper gifts that land
segments.narration: If your per-person number is small, it helps to know what actually lands. Consumables people would buy anyway, like good coffee or a favorite snack. Something you made or cooked. An experience you do together, like a hike and a picnic. A group gift where several people chip in for one thing someone actually wants. And for big families, suggest a name draw where everyone buys for one person. Most people are relieved when someone else suggests it first.
segments.on_screen_text: Gifts that work on a budget
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a small basket with a coffee bag, a jar of cookies and a handwritten card. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Deals without traps
segments.narration: Now the shopping itself. Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals can be real, but stores are designed to make you buy fast. Three rules. First, only buy things that were on your list before the sale. Second, check price history; some 'sale' prices are what the item cost in October. Third, use a cost-per-use test on anything for yourself: divide the price by how many times you'll realistically use it. A cheap thing you never use is the expensive one.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes with a short shopping list walking past a giant flashing sale sign. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Store cards and pay later
segments.narration: Two traps show up at checkout. The first is the store credit card offering twenty percent off today. Many store cards use deferred interest: if any balance is left when the promo ends, interest is charged all the way back to the purchase date, and store card rates are often near thirty percent. The second is buy now, pay later. One plan for something you could pay for today is fine. Five plans at once, each auto-pulling from a thin checking account, is how a fifty-dollar payment turns into a two-hundred-dollar week and a late fee. If you use it, one plan at a time.
segments.on_screen_text: Watch for store cards and BNPL stacking
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a checkout counter with a small store card and a stack of pay-in-four calendars, a caution sign beside them. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Pay with the right card
segments.narration: If you shop online, a credit card that you pay in full is usually safer than debit. With a credit card, a fraudulent charge is the bank's money while you dispute it, and federal law caps your liability at fifty dollars. With debit, the money leaves your checking right away. If you don't have a credit card, many banks offer virtual card numbers, and either way, turn on transaction alerts so you see every charge.

segments.heading: Track as you go
segments.narration: Tracking doesn't need an app. Put your four category numbers in your phone's notes app. Every time you buy something, subtract it. That's it. When a category hits zero, you stop or you move money from another category on purpose. If you want something more structured, the twenty-minute budget template in the description has a holiday section built in.

segments.heading: January plan
segments.narration: Finally, the part that makes next year easy. In early January, add up what you actually spent. Divide it by twelve. That's how much to put in a holiday sinking fund every month, starting with your first January paycheck. Set it as an automatic transfer to a separate savings account. Next November, the money is just there, and December stops being a financial event.

script.title: Credit scores explained from zero
script.hook: Your credit score affects your rent, your car loan, sometimes even your phone deposit. And nobody explains how it actually works. Let's fix that.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: Your credit score can affect whether you get an apartment, what rate you pay on a car, and whether you need a deposit for a phone plan or utilities. But most of us were never taught how it works. So this is credit from zero: what a report is, what a score is, the five things that move it, how to build it if you have nothing, how to fix errors, and the myths you can ignore. Grab a coffee. By the end, you'll know more than most adults.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes standing at a whiteboard with a simple score dial drawn on it. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Report vs score
segments.narration: First, two different things. Your credit report is a record: your accounts, balances, payment history, and inquiries, kept by three bureaus called Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. Your credit score is a number calculated from that report. There are many scoring models, but the most common is FICO, from 300 to 850. So the report is the raw data, and the score is a summary of it. Fix the report, and the score follows.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a page of simple lines on the left and a dial on the right connected by an arrow. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The five factors
segments.narration: FICO scores are built from five categories. Payment history is about thirty-five percent: do you pay on time? Amounts owed are about thirty percent, mostly how much of your credit limits you're using. Length of credit history is about fifteen percent. New credit, meaning recent applications, is about ten percent. And credit mix, the variety of account types, is about ten percent. Notice the first two add up to sixty-five percent. Two habits drive most of your score: pay on time and keep balances low.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a pie chart with five slices, the two biggest glowing. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Payment history
segments.narration: Payment history is the biggest piece, and it's the simplest. Pay at least the minimum by the due date, every time. A payment that's thirty or more days late can be reported and can stay on your report for up to seven years. The easiest protection: set up autopay for at least the minimum on every card and loan. Then pay more manually. Autopay is your seatbelt.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a calendar where every due date has a small green check. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Utilization
segments.narration: Amounts owed is mostly about utilization: your card balances divided by your card limits. If you have a $1,000 limit and a $300 balance, that's thirty percent. Lower is better, and people with the highest scores often use under ten percent. Here's the part almost nobody knows: the balance that gets reported is usually your statement balance. So you can pay in full every month and still show high utilization if you spend a lot before the statement closes. If that's you, make a payment a few days before the statement date.
segments.on_screen_text: Balance ÷ limit. Pay before the statement.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a credit card with a fill bar and a small calendar marking the statement date. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Age and new credit
segments.narration: Length of history rewards time, so keep your oldest no-annual-fee card open, even if you barely use it. Put one small subscription on it so the issuer doesn't close it for inactivity. New credit looks at recent applications. A hard inquiry usually costs fewer than five points, counts in FICO for about a year and drops off your report after two. And if you're shopping for a car loan or mortgage, multiple inquiries in a short window are treated as one, so compare offers.
segments.on_screen_text: Keep old cards. Space out applications.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. an old card with a candle and a few envelopes spaced along a timeline. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Building from nothing
segments.narration: No credit at all? You have three common ways in. A secured card, where your deposit becomes your limit. A student card, if you're in school. Or becoming an authorized user on the card of someone who always pays on time. Pick one, put a small recurring bill on it, set autopay to pay in full, and leave it alone. After about six months of history, most people have a score. Then, after a year or so of on-time payments, you can usually qualify for a regular card.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. three keys on a ring, each slightly different. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Check your reports
segments.narration: Now let's look at your actual reports. Go to AnnualCreditReport.com, the official free site, and get all three. Check four things. Are the personal details right? Do you recognize every account? Are any payments marked late that weren't? And are there inquiries you didn't make? A surprising number of reports contain mistakes, and some of those mistakes cost points.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. three report pages fanned out with a magnifying glass. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Fixing errors
segments.narration: If something's wrong, dispute it directly with the bureau that shows it. It's free, and you can do it online. Explain what's wrong and include any proof, like a statement showing an on-time payment. The bureau generally has thirty days to investigate. You do not need to pay a credit repair company for this. Anything legitimate they can do, you can do yourself for free. And if you see accounts you didn't open, that's possible identity theft: report it at IdentityTheft.gov and freeze your credit at all three bureaus.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes writing a letter with a small shield stamp on the envelope. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Myths
segments.narration: A few myths to drop. Checking your own score does not hurt it; that's a soft pull. You don't need to carry a balance to build credit; paying in full works just as well and costs nothing. Your income isn't part of your score. And closing a card doesn't erase its history right away, but it can raise your utilization, so think before closing your only cards.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a stack of speech bubbles being crossed out. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: So: your report is the data, your score is the summary. Sixty-five percent comes from paying on time and keeping balances low. Autopay the minimum on everything. Pay before the statement date if your balance runs high. Keep old cards open. Space out applications. Check your three reports for free and dispute errors yourself. Do that for a year, and your score mostly takes care of itself.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes giving a thumbs up beside a score dial pointing high. No text, no logos, no real people.

script.title: Your 401(k), explained: match, vesting, funds and fees
script.hook: If your job offers a 401(k), it might be the most valuable benefit you have, and most people set it up once in a hurry on their first day. Let's do it properly.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: If your job offers a 401(k), it might be the most valuable benefit you have. And most people set it up once, in a hurry, during onboarding, and never look at it again. So in this video, we'll go through the whole thing: how to get the full match, traditional versus Roth, vesting, how to pick a fund in about five minutes, fees, how to raise your contribution painlessly, and what to do when you change jobs. Have your 401(k) login handy.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes at a desk with a laptop and a small jar labeled with a simple building icon. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: What it is
segments.narration: A 401(k) is a retirement account through your employer. Money goes straight from your paycheck into the account before you ever see it, and it's invested in funds you choose. Because it comes out automatically, it's one of the easiest ways to save. There are annual contribution limits set by the IRS, and for 2026 the employee limit is 24,500 dollars, so most of us are nowhere near the ceiling.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a paycheck with an arrow into a jar with a small sprout. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The match
segments.narration: Many employers match part of what you put in. A common example: they match fifty percent of your contributions up to six percent of your salary. On a fifty-thousand-dollar salary, if you put in six percent, three thousand dollars, they add fifteen hundred. That's an instant fifty percent return on that money, before any investment growth. So step one, always: contribute at least enough to get the full match. Check your plan's exact formula in the benefits portal; they vary a lot.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. two coins dropping in, a second smaller coin following each one. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Traditional vs Roth
segments.narration: Many plans offer two versions. Traditional: money goes in before tax, which lowers your tax bill now, and you pay tax when you withdraw in retirement. Roth: money goes in after tax, and qualified withdrawals in retirement are tax-free. A rough rule: if you're early in your career and expect to earn more later, Roth is often attractive. If you're in a high bracket now, traditional may be better. Splitting between both is a perfectly reasonable answer when you're not sure.
segments.on_screen_text: Traditional = tax break now. Roth = later.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. two jars, one with a tax gate at the start and one with a tax gate opened at the end. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Vesting
segments.narration: Next, vesting. Your own contributions are always one hundred percent yours. But the employer match may vest over time. With cliff vesting, you get nothing until a certain date, then all of it, and that can't be more than three years. With graded vesting, you earn a percentage each year, fully vested by year six at the latest. Find your vested balance on your plan's website. If you're thinking about changing jobs, check your vesting date first. A few months can be worth thousands.
segments.on_screen_text: Your money: always yours. Match: may vest.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. two staircases, one single big step and one with small even steps. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Picking a fund
segments.narration: Now the part that freezes people: picking investments. Here's the five-minute version. Look for a target-date fund with the year closest to when you'll be about sixty-five. It holds a mix of stocks and bonds and adjusts automatically as you get older. One fund, done. If your plan's target-date funds are expensive, the alternative is a low-cost broad index fund, like a total market or S&P 500 index fund. What you want to avoid is leaving your money in a cash or money market default if your plan put it there, because cash barely grows over decades.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a single pie chart with a small calendar year flag on it. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Fees
segments.narration: Every fund has an expense ratio, a yearly fee as a percentage of your balance. You'll find it in the fund details. A broad index fund might charge well under a quarter of a percent. Some actively managed funds charge one percent or more. That difference sounds tiny, but over thirty or forty years it can cost you tens of thousands of dollars. When two funds do the same job, pick the cheaper one.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a small pair of scissors snipping a slice from a tall coin tower. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Raising your rate
segments.narration: Once you're getting the match, the goal is to slowly raise your contribution. The painless way: increase it by one percent every time you get a raise. A three percent raise minus one percent extra saving still means a bigger paycheck. Many plans also offer auto-escalation, which bumps your rate automatically every year. Turn it on once and forget it. A common long-term target is saving around fifteen percent of income for retirement, including the match, but any increase helps.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a staircase of coin stacks with a small dial clicking up each step. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Changing jobs
segments.narration: When you leave a job, you have choices for your old 401(k). You can usually leave it where it is, roll it into your new employer's plan, or roll it into an IRA. What you should almost never do is cash it out. You'd typically owe income tax plus a ten percent penalty if you're under fifty-nine and a half, and you lose all that future growth. If you roll it over, ask for a direct rollover so the money moves between accounts without being sent to you.
segments.on_screen_text: Leaving? Roll it, don't cash it.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes carrying a jar carefully from one building to another. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Mistakes
segments.narration: A few common mistakes. Not contributing enough to get the full match. Leaving money in the default cash option. Checking your balance every day and selling during a market drop. Borrowing from your 401(k) for non-emergencies. And never updating your beneficiary. Take two minutes to name one today; it's in your account settings.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a short list with five small warning triangles. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Recap. Contribute at least enough for the full match. Choose traditional, Roth, or both. Know your vesting schedule. Pick a target-date fund or a low-cost index fund, and check the expense ratio. Raise your contribution one percent with every raise or turn on auto-escalation. Never cash out when you change jobs. Do this today, and your future self will be very glad you did.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes looking at a tall jar on a long timeline with a calm smile. No text, no logos, no real people.

script.title: 10 money moves to make before January 1
script.hook: The last two weeks of December are the best time of year to fix your money, and it takes about an hour. Here are the ten moves, in order.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: The last weeks of December are quietly the best time of year to sort out your money. Some benefits expire, some deadlines are real, and setting things up now means January starts on autopilot. Here are ten moves. Each takes five to ten minutes. You can do them all in an afternoon, or one a day until New Year's.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes with a scarf and a clipboard, a small calendar showing late December. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 1. FSA
segments.narration: Move one: your FSA. If you have a health flexible spending account through work, log in and check your balance and deadline. These are generally use-it-or-lose-it, though some plans have a grace period or let you carry over a limited amount. Spend what's left on things you'd buy anyway: glasses, contacts, prescriptions, a dental visit, first aid supplies, many over-the-counter medicines.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a first aid kit, a glasses case and a pill bottle on a shelf. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 2. 401(k) rate
segments.narration: Move two: your 401(k) contribution rate for next year. Make sure you're getting the full employer match. If you got a raise this year, bump your rate by one percent. Contributions for this tax year have to come out of this year's paychecks, so if you wanted to put in more for this year, check with payroll now before the last paycheck runs.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a dial clicking up one notch. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 3. Withholding
segments.narration: Move three: run the free IRS Tax Withholding Estimator. With a recent pay stub, it takes about fifteen minutes and tells you if you're headed for a big refund or a bill. If something's off, it helps you fill out a new W-4 to give to payroll for January. Especially do this if you started a side gig, changed jobs or got married this year.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a calculator with a small envelope and a pay stub. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 4. Credit check
segments.narration: Move four: credit. Pull your free credit reports at AnnualCreditReport.com and scan them for accounts you don't recognize or late payments that aren't right. While you're there, consider a credit freeze at all three bureaus. It's free, it doesn't affect your score, and it blocks most new-account fraud. You can unfreeze in minutes when you need to apply for something.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. three report pages and a small snowflake-shaped lock. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 5. Subscriptions
segments.narration: Move five: subscriptions. Open your bank and card statements from the last three months and list every recurring charge. Cancel anything you didn't use this fall. Be ruthless with free trials you signed up for during holiday sales; they're about to start charging.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. scissors cutting a chain of small recurring icons. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 6. Perks
segments.narration: Move six: work perks you haven't used. Some employers offer learning stipends, wellness reimbursements, phone or internet allowances, or commuter benefits that reset with the calendar year. Check your benefits portal or ask HR. It's money you've already earned.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a gift ribbon on a small company building. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 7. Net worth
segments.narration: Move seven: write down your net worth. Add up everything you own, cash, investments, retirement accounts and your car at resale value, then subtract what you owe. Negative because of student loans? Normal in your twenties. This is a baseline, so next December you can see how far you've come.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a notebook with a simple scale drawing. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 8. Big known costs
segments.narration: Move eight: list next year's known big costs. Car registration, insurance renewals, annual subscriptions, weddings you're invited to, travel, the holidays themselves. These aren't surprises. They're on the calendar. Write each one down with its month and amount.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a calendar with small icons on different months. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 9. Sinking funds
segments.narration: Move nine: turn that list into sinking funds. Divide each cost by the number of months until it's due and set up an automatic transfer to a separate savings account. Six hundred dollars of travel in June, starting in January, is a hundred dollars a month. Now those costs come from savings instead of a credit card.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a row of small jars, each filling at its own pace. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 10. Three goals
segments.narration: Move ten: pick three money goals for next year, each with a number, a date and an automatic action. Not 'save more', but 'twenty-four hundred dollars in my emergency fund by December, a hundred dollars every payday'. Set the automations before January 1. Then put a check-in on your calendar at the end of each quarter.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. three gold stars pinned to a board. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Deadlines
segments.narration: Two deadlines worth remembering. 401(k) contributions for this year come from this year's paychecks, so December is your last chance. IRA and HSA contributions for this tax year can generally be made until the tax filing deadline in April. So if you want to make a Roth IRA contribution for this year, you still have a few months.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. two calendars side by side, December and April. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: So: spend the FSA, set your 401(k) rate, run the withholding estimator, check your credit and consider a freeze, cancel subscriptions, use your perks, write down net worth, list next year's big costs, start sinking funds, and set three automated goals. Ten moves, about an hour, and January starts with a plan.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes checking the last box on a list with a small party popper. No text, no logos, no real people.
